RISC-V processors are being considered for use in edge computing due to their potential for low power consumption and flexibility. To further reduce power usage in these devices, we was curious about exploring the feasibility of implementing a highly power-constrained CPU architecture that operates at extremely low frequencies. Typically, CPUs function effectively at frequencies ranging from 1 to 3 GHz. In contrast, our HyperDegrade architecture succeeds in performing computations at microwaves frequency, specifically 13.56 MHz, following an initial high-frequency processing stage. We achieved this success by devoting specific tasks to either the primary or secondary processor, utilizing a low-frequency CPU for simple instructions and a high-frequency one for complicated ones. Furthermore, our design incorporates a radio-frequency identification (RFID) based data transfer method to connect the two processors. To evaluate our HyperDegrade architecture, we developed a prototype consisting of a main CPU operating at 13.56 MHz and a secondary one operating at 200 MHz. The results showed that our architecture is capable of executing Linux operating systems at both low and high frequencies. The 13.56 MHz CPU delivers a performance of 1.23 GOPS and uses 2.47 mW of power, whereas the 200 MHz CPU delivers a performance of 24.6 GOPS and uses 237 mW of power. The data transfer between the two processors occurs within 50 microseconds. The HyperDegrade architecture provides a groundbreaking approach to designing extremely low-power CPUs that operate at microwave frequencies for implementation in various edge computing applications. A noise spike that occurs during the failure of a material under stress has been found to signal the onset of a subsequent failure when the stress is increased. A system that generates noise as a result of failure under stress, similar to the aforementioned experiments, has been proposed. Within this proposed system, the noise spike predictor plays a crucial role in determining whether the current failure event indicates the beginning of a new failure or the end of the failure sequence. If the event signifies the start of a new failure, the predictor directs the learning model to update the information regarding the current failure. If, however, the event indicates the end of the failure sequence, the predictor instructs the model to prepare for the potential onset of an upcoming failure by updating the information regarding the upcoming failure. If the noise spike indicates the onset of a new failure, the model needs to be updated accordingly to determine the initial parameters of the new failure. If the event signifies the end of the failure sequence, the model updates the information regarding the final failure. Using a linear stability analysis, we evaluate the VSI growth rate in a variety of disk models with different particle distribution heights.
